analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from issuing rules or health assessments unless every underlying scientific dataset is made public.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 7 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the EPA from proposing, finalizing, or releasing any risk assessment, standard, regulation, or guidance unless every piece of scientific and technical information behind it — raw data, protocols, computer codes, and models — was specifically identified and publicly available enough for outsiders to independently analyze and reproduce the results. On its face this is a transparency requirement. In practice, much of the key evidence behind federal air-pollution and public-health rules comes from long-term epidemiology studies whose raw data contain confidential patient medical records that privacy law forbids releasing, so the bill would have made much of that evidence unusable and given regulated industries a new way to challenge or delay EPA standards in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by EPA air, water, and chemical standards would benefit most. Any rule or assessment they disliked could be challenged on the ground that some underlying data or computer code was not fully public or reproducible, adding years of delay and litigation before standards took effect. The bill's stated beneficiaries were the public, through greater scrutiny of the science behind federal rules.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the EPA to specifically identify and publicly release all scientific and technical information behind any covered action, including raw data, protocols, computer codes, and models, before proposing, finalizing, or disseminating it.
The stated aim was to let outside parties independently analyze and substantially reproduce the research results EPA relies on, so that no federal standard would rest on data the public cannot see.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost in slower or weaker health and environmental protections: air-quality standards and hazard assessments that rest on confidential medical data could be blocked outright, and those that survived would face new legal attacks. The public's interest in seeing the science behind rules was the stated purpose, but the mechanism traded that transparency against the speed and strength of the protections themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to air and water pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill would have barred EPA from relying on landmark public-health research whose raw data include confidential patient medical records that privacy law forbids releasing, so the agency could have been unable to use the core evidence behind its major air-quality standards.

By making every rule or assessment legally vulnerable if any data or computer code were judged not sufficiently reproducible, the bill would have created a new route for regulated industries to delay or overturn standards in court, slowing protections for years.

Supporters of transparency have a real point: the public should be able to scrutinize the science behind major rules. An honest supporter of this bill would have to acknowledge, though, that the carve-out for data whose disclosure is prohibited by law was vague, leaving unclear how much of the key evidence would actually have been covered and how disputes would be resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency goal is legitimate on its face: people affected by federal rules should be able to see the evidence behind them. But the requirement was drawn broadly enough that it would sweep in studies whose raw data cannot lawfully be made public, and the bill offered no clear process for handling those cases. The likely practical effect was not better science but fewer and slower health and environmental standards, with the disputes resolved by regulated industries in court. A narrower bill limited to truly withheld data, or one funding secure ways to let outside experts review confidential data without publishing it, would have gotten closer to the stated goal without the same cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2014, and with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015, it simply expired.

narrative.text: The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on July 16, 2014, and the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
Support never expanded beyond its original eight Republican sponsors; no Democrat cosponsored the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the EPA's existing authority to set health and environmental standards was left untouched, and regulated industries did not gain the new legal tool it would have created. People who rely on air and water protections were better off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA authority and existing health safeguards

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Secret Science Reform Act on July 16, 2014.

for.name: Sens. Vitter, Enzi, Inhofe, Risch, Flake, Fischer, and Crapo

against.name: Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred; the action history shows no committee action beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: All eight senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Republicans; no Democrat joined, and the bill never moved in the Democratic-led committee.

industries.industry: Regulated polluting industries (fossil fuels, power plants, manufacturers and chemical firms subject to EPA standards)
industries.note: The bill would have made it far easier to challenge or stall EPA rules by arguing that the underlying research data was not fully public or reproducible. That would raise the cost and delay of every major environmental standard, at the expense of the people those standards protect.

Long-term epidemiology studies, which supply much of the evidence for pollution standards, depend on confidential patient records. A requirement to publish all raw data would have limited which studies EPA could legally rely on and chilled the research those standards rest on.
